semantic_correction.stem: Immediately after rupture of membranes during labor, the fetal heart rate drops abruptly. On vaginal examination, the nurse palpates a pulsating umbilical cord below the presenting part. Which action should the nurse take?

options.A: Call for obstetric help and manually elevate the presenting part off the cord while emergency delivery is prepared.
options.B: Gently push the prolapsed cord back above the presenting part and continue labor once the cord is no longer visible.
options.C: Apply firm fundal pressure to speed fetal descent while the team prepares for delivery and monitors the fetal heart rate.
options.D: Remove the examining hand and place the client supine while waiting for the obstetric team to decide on the delivery plan.

semantic_correction.rationale: Umbilical cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency because compression of the cord can rapidly reduce fetal oxygen delivery. Current NCBI guidance states that the diagnosis is clinical when a pulsating cord is palpable or visible and may be accompanied by fetal bradycardia, particularly after rupture of membranes. Until expedient delivery can occur, the cornerstone of management is funic decompression by manually elevating the fetal presenting part off the cord. Emergency obstetric assistance and preparation for rapid delivery, usually cesarean when vaginal birth is not immediately imminent, should occur simultaneously. Routine manual replacement of the prolapsed cord is not recommended because manipulation can provoke vasospasm or recurrent prolapse. Fundal pressure can worsen cord compression, and removing the hand or leaving the client supine while awaiting a plan abandons decompression. The 2026 NCSBN NCLEX-RN Test Plan includes care for complications of labor and delivery and emergency/complication intervention under Physiological Adaptation. Therefore A is the uniquely best response.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: When umbilical cord prolapse is identified, immediately relieve cord compression by elevating the presenting part and summon the obstetric team while urgent delivery is prepared.

Rebuilt the UID into a high-value obstetric emergency requiring immediate decompression of a prolapsed umbilical cord while urgent delivery is prepared.

audit_findings_append.finding: The replacement tests immediate maternal-fetal emergency action. NCBI directly supports manual elevation of the presenting part and urgent delivery preparation for cord prolapse.

scope_exclusions.delivery_interval: No decision-to-delivery or incision time target is asserted; the item tests immediate decompression and urgent delivery preparation.
scope_exclusions.bladder_filling: No bladder-instillation volume or technique is prescribed. Manual elevation is sufficient to test the immediate nursing priority.
scope_exclusions.tocolysis: No tocolytic agent, dose, route, or indication is tested.
scope_exclusions.cord_handling: The item does not direct routine manual replacement of the cord into the uterus and avoids excessive manipulation that may contribute to vasospasm.

near_duplicate_check.note: Targeted GitHub search for 'umbilical cord prolapse fetal bradycardia elevate presenting part emergency cesarean' returned no indexed repository match. No broad bank rescan was performed.

option_audit.A: Correct. It relieves mechanical cord compression immediately while the obstetric team prepares definitive delivery.
option_audit.B: Plausible attempt to restore cord position, but routine funic reduction is not recommended and manipulation can provoke vasospasm or recurrent prolapse.
option_audit.C: Plausible attempt to hasten birth, but fundal pressure can increase presenting-part pressure on the prolapsed cord and worsen fetal compromise.
option_audit.D: Plausible if waiting for definitive obstetric direction, but removing decompression and using a supine position can allow ongoing cord compression during a fetal emergency.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible best answer. A combines immediate decompression with emergency escalation. B manipulates/replaces the cord, C increases compression risk, and D abandons decompression while delaying definitive action.

cueing_check.note: Exact character counts were calculated from the stored strings. The correct option is not longest and all four choices are parallel obstetric emergency actions.

blueprint_audit.entry_level_relevance: NCSBN Physiological Adaptation directly includes care for labor/delivery complications and emergency intervention. Immediate recognition and decompression of cord prolapse are direct entry-level RN responsibilities in obstetric care.
